title: CellPlex: Benchmarking Single-Cell Spatial Proteomics Prediction from H&E
abstract: Spatial proteomics measures tens of proteins in every cell of a tissue section, but its cost confines it to small research cohorts, whereas hematoxylin and eosin (H\&E) slides exist for nearly every patient. Inferring single-cell spatial proteomics from H\&E would bring its analyses to routine pathology, and a growing number of virtual staining models pursue this goal. Each is evaluated on its own cohort, panel and pixel-level metric, and released models transfer poorly to new cohorts, leaving open which approach to build on and which proteins H\&E can reveal. We introduce CellPlex, a benchmark that poses the task at the level of the cell: seven cohorts with same-section H\&E and multiplexed immunofluorescence, from colorectal and breast cancer to lymph-node metastases, bone marrow and glioma, with 717 samples, 44.8 million cells and 149 proteins, processed by one pipeline into per-cell targets. Pathology foundation models (PFMs) are adapted with one cell-level protocol, specialist models are fine-tuned under a matched budget, and all are scored on the same cells. Adapted PFMs are the most accurate models on every cohort, ahead of the specialists even after fine-tuning, but keep less than half of their accuracy on cohorts they were not trained on. Which proteins can be predicted depends on the tissue, not on how many cells were measured for them. By fixing the cells, targets and splits on which predictions are judged, CellPlex sets a common standard for inferring costly molecular measurements from routine H\&E and shows how far H\&E can stand in for spatial proteomics. We will release the data, splits, evaluation code and baselines as a testbed for developing and comparing future pathology foundation models and virtual staining methods.

title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
abstract: Comprehensively characterizing cellular landscapes to elucidate cell diversity is a central goal in biology. Recent advances in single-cell profiling have created unprecedented opportunities for this endeavor by capturing diverse transcriptomes with remarkable breadth. However, current foundation models generally struggle to leverage such holistic and valuable information to represent a cell. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression into a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million image-based cell profiles across 40 species and covering over one million genes, CellNet improves the recognition of rare and condition-associated cellular states, enables the study of genes beyond experimentally measured panels, and uncovers associations between poorly characterized non-coding RNAs and known biological programmes. CellNet paves the way for AI-enabled cell-biology discovery at the whole-transcriptome scale. The CellNet website is available at https://www.cellnet.top.

title: Radiation-Induced Intracranial Aneurysm After Cranial Radiation Therapy: Hemodynamic Considerations in a Long-Term Glioblastoma Survivor.
abstract: Long-term survival after glioblastoma (GB) remains uncommon; however, advances in genomic research and contemporary multimodal therapy have increased the number of long-term survivors. In these patients, late effects of cranial radiation therapy may accumulate over time, affecting cognitive and endocrine function and increasing the risk of cerebrovascular disorders and secondary malignancies. We report a long-term GB survivor who developed multiple late radiation-related complications, including radiation-induced intracranial aneurysm (RIA). During the clinical course of this case, serial imaging demonstrated that hemodynamic stress secondary to proximal large-artery stenosis/occlusion contributed to aneurysm formation. This observation suggests that cerebrovascular risk after cranial irradiation cannot be assessed solely on the basis of radiation dose distribution and that hemodynamic stress may play a contributory role in RIA development. This case highlights 2 important clinical implications. First, late radiation-related complications may accumulate in the same long-term GB survivor and become critical determinants of outcome. Second, cerebrovascular risk cannot be assessed based on radiation dose distribution alone, and the effects of hemodynamic stress should be considered. With advances in genomics and contemporary care increasing the number of long-term survivors, the incidence of postradiation therapy complications is likely to rise. To reduce preventable morbidity, surveillance should extend beyond tumor control to include longitudinal vascular assessment, with explicit attention to hemodynamic warning signs, such as new arterial stenoses, evolving collateral pathways, and de novo or enlarging aneurysms.

title: Traumatic brain injury: Multi-omics insights into brain aging, neurodegeneration, and precision therapeutics.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of mortality and persistent neurological disability and is increasingly recognized as a potential contributor to accelerated brain aging and long-term neurodegenerative processes. Beyond the immediate mechanical insult, TBI initiates dynamic secondary injury cascades involving chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic and axonal degeneration, metabolic disturbances, and blood-brain barrier disruption. The persistence and temporal evolution of these molecular alterations may interact with intrinsic aging mechanisms, contributing to progressive neuronal dysfunction and increased vulnerability to age-associated neurodegenerative disorders. The marked biological and temporal heterogeneity of TBI therefore presents major challenges for conventional diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic approaches. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and single-cell and spatial approaches, offer unprecedented opportunities to characterize the molecular trajectories linking TBI, brain aging, and neurodegeneration. Integrative multi-omics frameworks, coupled with network biology, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and causal inference, enable the identification of molecular signatures, age-related regulatory networks, clinically relevant biomarkers, and therapeutically actionable targets. This review synthesizes emerging multi-omics insights into the molecular mechanisms through which TBI may influence brain aging and neurodegenerative progression, with particular emphasis on phase-specific molecular signatures, biomarker discovery, patient stratification, therapeutic target prioritization, and precision neurotherapeutics. We further discuss longitudinal profiling, single-cell and spatial approaches, and AI-assisted modeling for patient stratification and therapeutic optimization. Integrating multi-omics with systems biology may provide a framework for studying TBI-associated brain aging and developing personalized interventions, although prospective clinical validation remains essential.

title: Artificial intelligence for predicting BCG response in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer: a systematic review.
abstract: To systematically identify, appraise and synthesise artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) models that predict treatment response and clinical outcomes after intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), a setting in which current risk calculators underperform, and identifying non-responders has become urgent as alternatives to BCG enter practice. PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science were searched through April 2026 following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews [PROSPERO] number CRD420261376808). Studies developing or validating AI/ML models for BCG-associated outcomes with a quantitative performance metric were included. Risk of bias was assessed with the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST). Evidence was synthesised along a clinically oriented framework: AI as a perceptual tool (extracting signal from histology or imaging) or integrative tool (re-weighting clinicopathological, molecular, or urinary variables). A total of 15 studies (>24 900 patients) were included: seven perceptual, eight integrative. By input data, six used digital pathology, two radiomics, two genomics/transcriptomics, four clinicopathological markers, and one urinary biomarkers. The digital-pathology Computational Histology Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) platform, validated across 12 international centres, stratified high-grade recurrence (hazard ratio [HR] 2.08), progression (HR 3.87) and BCG-unresponsive disease (HR 2.31), and was the only model providing a first signal of predictive value, demonstrating a significant BCG vs gemcitabine/docetaxel interaction (P = 0.029). Integrative models PROGRxN-BCa (concordance index [C-index] 0.79) and DeepSurv (C-index 0.881) outperformed standard calculators but with modest gains (ΔC-index 0.05-0.10). Only 40% of studies performed external validation, none prospectively; five were at high risk of bias. Perceptual AI, particularly digital pathology, has the highest external validation and provides the only biomarker with a first signal of predictive value for BCG vs alternatives, increasingly relevant in the context of the global BCG shortage. Integrative models such as PROGRxN-BCa and DeepSurv outperform standard calculators with incremental gains and are freely accessible. Prospective validation, systematic calibration reporting and treatment-by-biomarker interaction analyses, ideally embedded in trials such as the BRIDGE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05538663), remain priorities before clinical adoption.

title: AI-Driven Multiomics Biomarkers for Precision Oncology: Navigating the Translational Gap and Regulatory Hurdles.
abstract: The discussion on precision oncology integrates multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence, specifically addressing biomarker discovery and personalized therapeutic strategies. In this way, clinical translation and multiomics biomarkers are reconstructed challenges such as heterogeneity, validate, algorithmic bias, regulatory complexities, and ethical issues. This review critically evaluates how advanced technologies operating in an integrated manner facilitate precision oncology by supporting fields such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and radiomics. To conduct the study, we performed literature search using standard databases such as PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, focusing on papers published between 2020 and 2025. We address the all aspects of biomarker identification and clinical applications; we employed a five-stage framework comprising multiparametric data generation, integration, biomarker discovery, rigorous validation, and regulatory implementation. To further examine this review, we have employed emerging computational approaches, including machine learning and deep learning and graph neural networks alongside regulatory frameworks and ethical, legal, and social considerations. Discussing translation barriers, we consider factors such as limited reproducibility, validation, and critical discussion particularly studies. Ultimately, a future model based on standardized, validated, and transparent learning strategies accelerates and fosters the development of clinically reliable standards. Our review provides an integrative roadmap for modern, multiomics-driven biomarker approaches in precision oncology practice.

## 局限与风险
该研究属于弱AI交叉的综述，并非原发性研究。局限性在于缺乏具体的实验细节和新算法的性能指标（摘要未说明具体的准确率或召回率提升）。风险点在于，综述所涵盖的2020-2025年文献可能存在发表偏倚，且文中提到的“未来模型”仍处于理论构建阶段，缺乏在大规模临床队列中的前瞻性验证证据。

title: Artificial intelligence in pediatric nephrology: current applications and emerging frameworks for evidence generation.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming many areas of medicine. Pediatric nephrology may be a field of particular relevance due to its data-rich environments, rarity of diseases, long-term follow-up needs, and persistent evidence gaps. Traditional clinical research methods, including randomized controlled trials, are often difficult to conduct in pediatric nephrology because of small sample sizes, ethical constraints, heterogeneity of disease, and long latency to clinically meaningful outcomes. AI-based methods offer complementary approaches to address these challenges, spanning diagnostic support, prognostic modeling, imaging analysis, treatment personalization, and innovative frameworks for evidence generation. This narrative review provides a focused overview of AI applications that are already available or emerging in pediatric nephrology, integrating lessons from broader nephrology research on real-world data and digital-twin technologies. We refer to established and near-term applications in chronic kidney disease, dialysis, transplantation, imaging, pathology, and genomics in children. We then discuss future directions, including AI-enabled virtual trials and digital twins as potential tools to extend evidence to pediatric populations traditionally excluded from trials. Ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations specific to children are highlighted. We conclude that AI should be viewed as an adjunct, rather than a replacement to conventional clinical research, with particular promise for advancing precision, inclusivity, and timeliness of evidence in pediatric nephrology.

title: QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution
abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.

title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.

title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance
abstract: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints. However, different agents support different instruction formats, and limited empirical evidence exists about how these files are adopted, what information they contain, whether coexisting formats provide consistent guidance, and how they are maintained. We conduct an empirical study of 3,387 instruction files from 1,000 GitHub repositories across four formats: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules. We find that 42.2% of instruction-bearing repositories in the higher-popularity cohort maintain multiple formats. Among 386 manually examined pairs of corresponding sections, 16.1% provide divergent guidance. Our maintenance analysis further shows that 40.4% of the analyzed files have only one recorded modification event and that maintenance patterns differ across formats. Based on category prevalence and category addition ratios (CAR), we derive an evidence-based template containing ten Required, four Gap, and two Recommended categories. In an exploratory generation experiment, explicit template guidance increases structural category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8%. We further introduce AGIT-Instruct, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-file generation through structural coverage and content alignment. Across four generation configurations, retrieval-augmented generation achieves the highest full-file ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.459. A manual assessment of 278 generated category instances finds that 19.4% fully preserve and 61.2% partially preserve developer-written intent. Our findings provide empirical guidance for organizing and maintaining agent instruction

title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling
abstract: LLM-based applications often employ agentic workflows and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which build long prompts from shared context. When prefixes are shared across requests, serving engines reuse the key-value (KV) cache to skip parts of the prefill computation. Reuse is typically graded: the uncached work of requests in a queue can differ by up to 100x. In this setting, the order of scheduling determines the time-to-first-token (TTFT) for the queued requests. KV reuse-first scheduling, which prioritizes the requests with the longest KV cache hit, gives the lowest median TTFT but starves expensive requests under load spikes; first-come-first-served (FCFS) scheduling bounds the tail but raises the median TTFT. We present Fairway, a prefill scheduler built on adaptive reuse prioritization: it favors KV cache reuse while queues are short, and shifts toward fair allocation as requests wait longer relative to their own prefill time. Fairway employs a virtual dual lane model: a KV reuse-first Fast lane and a Fair lane atop the serving engine's waiting queue that enables speeding up of cheap reuse requests without starving expensive ones. This model automatically adapts to the workload without any per-workload tuning. Fairway lowers the tail TTFT at no cost to the median in transient overload. Across workloads and load levels, Fairway matches or beats the best baseline, with a p99 TTFT up to 8.6x lower than prior prefix-aware schedulers. During load spikes, it keeps the tail of FCFS at a 6x lower median TTFT.

title: Reliability Stress Testing of RAG Retrieval under Query-Relevant Corpus Poisoning
abstract: External text can affect a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system only after the retriever admits it to the model context. We stress this admission step while varying document content, attacker query information, per-target poison budget, and contamination scope. Across 623 Benchmarking Information Retrieval (BEIR) queries from SciFact and NFCorpus, five query-targeted documents per query reduce classical-retriever nDCG@10 by 40.2-61.5% in isolated-target stress. Full-query anchoring explains most Best Matching 25 (BM25) degradation, whereas appended text also shifts latent semantic analysis (LSA) and Hybrid rankings. A pretrained BGE-small validation reaches 100% target exposure for query-only P=5 on both datasets; adding the injection payload changes SciFact nDCG only from 0.269 to 0.271 and lowers NFCorpus exposure slightly to 98.8%, indicating that query anchoring remains the dominant retrieval-side factor for this dense model. Query length materially changes the interpretation of partial-information attacks: on 162 long SciFact queries, two random terms cover 19.9% of eligible terms and still yield 39.5% Hybrid target exposure. Multi-target contamination adds cross-target interference. Overlap-based admission can remove full-query poisons but may sharply reduce clean retrieval utility, and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) leaves exposure unchanged under the tested configuration. The study measures retrieval-layer failures, not downstream instruction following.

title: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning
abstract: Power-grid customer service increasingly relies on community social media, where customers describe outages, billing, and equipment faults in informal regional dialect. Such messages exhibit non-standard morphology, semantic drift, and out-of-vocabulary expressions that make manual lexicon construction costly and degrade conventional NLP tools. We propose a weak-supervision framework constructing a regional slang lexicon from curated dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms. Candidates are generated via Pointwise Mutual Information with soft-label bidirectional anchoring, retaining dialect-anchored terms while recording power-domain relevance as separate metadata, and are scored by combining Sentence-BERT semantic similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure. Uncertainty-aware active learning with rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles is applied under three query strategies, and the resulting lexicon is evaluated by a higher-capability LLM calibrated against human expert annotations via Cohen's $κ$. On 11,177 real WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan, China), the framework achieves an evaluator-estimated dialect precision of DP~$=$~1.0 with zero false positives. An ablation shows that soft-label layering retains 751\% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the candidate pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration ($n=46$) yields $κ_{\text{dialect}}=1.0$ and $κ_{\text{power}}=0.85$. The resulting 25--33-term lexicon, 4--5 of which are power-relevant, provides a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.

title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.

title: From Scientific Observations to Mechanisms: Benchmarking Hypothesis Generation by AI Scientists
abstract: Data-driven mechanistic hypotheses are essential to scientific discovery because they explain how underlying processes produce observed phenomena. AI agents and AI scientists increasingly support scientific data analysis. However, their ability to turn empirical findings into mechanistic hypotheses remains insufficiently examined. To address this gap, we introduce MechHypoBench, the first benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate such hypotheses from empirical data. It combines paper-derived mechanisms from 14 scientific fields with real-world datasets containing 17.98 million records. The construction retains the observational complexity of empirical data while providing a specified underlying mechanism. Agents analyze the observations and propose open-form hypotheses. We develop an evaluation framework that assesses open-form mechanistic hypotheses through their consequences under withheld conditions. Experiments with general agents and AI scientists reveal a substantial gap between generated hypotheses and the underlying mechanisms.

title: SemFlowRAG: Directed Semantic Flow from Abstraction to Evidence for Complex Reasoning
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhanced by Knowledge Graphs has shown promise in complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. However, existing graph-based retrieval methods typically rely on flat, undirected topologies. During the retrieval process, the probability flow often gets trapped in high-degree abstract concept nodes which we define as ``probability black holes'', leading to semantic drift and noise accumulation. To address this, we propose SemFlowRAG, a framework that reconstructs the flat retrieval space into a corpus-adaptive semantic gradient graph. This data-driven self-organization enables a hierarchical structure to emerge naturally from the data distribution, capturing the intrinsic semantic granularity of the corpus to suppress structural noise. By quantifying the semantic abstractness of entities through the embedding variance of their associated passages, we transform static undirected edges into directed semantic constraints. Furthermore, we design an abstractness-guided directed PageRank algorithm that forces the retrieval trajectory to follow a ``high-to-low semantic abstractness'' gradient. This mechanism ensures layer-by-layer evidence convergence, smoothly guiding the retrieval process from abstract concepts to specific document evidence. Extensive experiments on complex QA datasets demonstrate that SemFlowRAG effectively mitigates the ``probability black holes'' issue, outperforming existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream reasoning performance.

title: Retrieval-Enhanced Cultural Evaluation for Social Media Translation Training
abstract: Social media translation requires preserving meaning while capturing the cultural nuances of user-generated content (UGC). However, gaps in the cultural knowledge of LLM-based evaluators can lead to inaccurate assessments and unreliable training rewards. To improve these signals, we use retrieval-enhanced cultural evaluation to train CUE-MT, a family of social media translation models. A calibrated, domain-specific Judger guides supervised data refinement and is augmented by an Agent for hard-example mining and reinforcement learning. The Agent retrieves relevant external evidence as needed and distills it into concise hints that the Judger uses to score translations and assign rewards. Across 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B backbones, CUE-MT outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines of comparable size on CUE-MT-Bench and three public benchmarks. Human evaluation on CUE-MT-Bench shows cultural effectiveness gains of 7.44-15.12 percentage points over the strongest external baseline in each size group. Retrieval improves the Judger's four-way classification accuracy by 8.07 percentage points over a matched no-retrieval baseline that uses LLM-generated hints alone. Training ablations further support the combination of hard-example mining and Agent-enhanced rewards.

title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.
